title: Ζεὺς καὶ χελώνη
source: Émile Chambry, Ésope: Fables, texte établi et traduit (Les Belles Lettres, Paris, 1927), fable 125 (= Perry 106). Text as printed, including Chambry's editorial punctuation (« »). Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; accents omitted).

sentences.t: Ζεὺς γαμῶν πάντα τὰ ζῷα εἱστία.
sentences.tr: Zeus gamōn panta ta zōia heistia.
sentences.l: Zeus, marrying, was feasting all the animals.
sentences.i: When Zeus married, he gave a feast for all the animals.
sentences.n: ἑστιάω is to receive a guest at one's hearth, ἑστία, and so to entertain at table. The imperfect εἱστία sets the banquet going and holds it open, which is what lets the next sentence notice who is missing.

sentences.t: Μόνης δὲ χελώνης ὑστερησάσης, διαπορῶν τὴν αἰτίαν, τῇ ὑστεραίᾳ ἐπυνθάνετο αὐτῆς διὰ τί μόνη ἐπὶ τὸ δεῖπνον οὐκ ἦλθε.
sentences.tr: Monēs de chelōnēs hysterēsasēs, diaporōn tēn aitian, tēi hysteraiāi epynthaneto autēs dia ti monē epi to deipnon ouk ēlthe.
sentences.l: But the tortoise alone having failed to come, being at a loss for the reason, on the following day he asked her why she alone had not come to the dinner.
sentences.n: Genitive absolute once more. ὑστερέω is to be behind time, and so to miss a thing altogether; ἡ ὑστεραία, the day after, is the same root — she was late, and he enquires the next day. πυνθάνομαι takes the genitive of the person enquired of, αὐτῆς.

sentences.t: Τῆς δὲ εἰπούσης· « Οἶκος φίλος, οἶκος ἄριστος, » ἀγανακτήσας κατ’ αὐτῆς παρεσκεύασεν αὐτὴν τὸν οἶκον αὐτὸν βαστάζουσαν περιφέρειν.
sentences.tr: Tēs de eipousēs· « Oikos philos, oikos aristos, » aganaktēsas kat’ autēs pareskeuasen autēn ton oikon auton bastazousan peripherein.
sentences.l: And when she had said: « Home dear, home best, » he, having grown angry at her, arranged that she should carry about the house itself, bearing it.
sentences.i: And when she said: « Home is dear, home is best, » he grew angry with her and arranged that she should carry that very house about with her wherever she went.
sentences.n: « Οἶκος φίλος, οἶκος ἄριστος » is quoted as a proverb and keeps a proverb's shape: no verb at all, the two halves simply set side by side, since Greek needs no 'is'. βαστάζω is to take up a weight and hold it, περιφέρω to carry it round about; between them they are the tortoise's shell. The fable is an aetiology — a story told to account for why the creature is as we see it.

sentences.t: Οὕτω πολλοὶ τῶν ἀνθρώπων αἱροῦνται μᾶλλον λιτῶς οἰκεῖν ἢ παρ’ ἄλλοις πολυτελῶς διαιτᾶσθαι.
sentences.tr: Houtō polloi tōn anthrōpōn hairountai mallon litōs oikein ē par’ allois polytelōs diaitasthai.
sentences.l: Thus many among men choose rather to dwell plainly than to live sumptuously at other people's.
sentences.n: αἱροῦνται μᾶλλον … ἤ is the regular way of saying 'prefer … to'. λιτός is plain and unadorned, of food and of furniture. διαιτάομαι is to pass one's life; παρ’ ἄλλοις is 'at other people's houses'. The moral takes the tortoise's proverb at its word, where Zeus took it as an insult.
